title: Length, comparison and buffer limits
goal: Validate the input as a C string within the buffer, then compare the whole key.

prerequisites.text: Be able to distinguish a complete record from truncation and find the terminating null within a char array.

terms.title: Key
terms.definition: A predefined text value that identifies a command.

terms.title: Prefix
terms.definition: The opening bytes of a string. The first two bytes of OK! form prefix OK.

terms.title: strcmp
terms.definition: Compares two C strings and returns a negative value, zero or a positive value.

terms.title: strlen
terms.definition: Counts bytes before the first '\0' and returns a size_t.

sections.title: The device has a command dictionary
paragraphs: A controller expects keys OK and ADJ. An operator types OK! out of habit. Its first two letters match, but the third byte changes the command. The device needs the whole key.
Separate a complete, valid input record from a rejected one first. After establishing that the array contains its '\0', the text is ready for strcmp and strlen.
A declaration char text[9] reserves nine cells. Eight can hold text bytes, with a cell left for '\0' after the input. In that buffer OK still has length two.

sections.title: Read the result of strcmp
paragraphs: Two arrays hold REF, and a third holds REF!. Equal strings compare as zero. Then compare the shorter string with a longer string that shares its first three bytes.
steps: key and reading match across three letters and each has '\0' at the next cell. strcmp returns zero, so the output is equal.
The first three bytes of key and longer match. At position 3, the comparison sees zero and the nonzero byte !.
Only the sign of the second result matters. The expression < 0 holds, so the output is before.

sections.title: Prefix matching gives another result
paragraphs: strncmp with a count of 2 examines at most two bytes. This test accepts OK!, since both opening bytes match. strcmp checks the full key, including that OK already has '\0' in cell 2.
strcmp takes two arguments. Clang rejects a call that also supplies a byte count. The separate function strncmp takes that count.

sections.title: Plan command tests
paragraphs: A new controller accepts RUN and STOP. List the exact strings and add an input with an extra character for which prefix matching would produce the wrong answer.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Check strcmp, strncmp and strlen contracts and the definition of a string.

selfcheck.prompt: When strcmp compares two strings REF and you test its return value for equality with zero, what happens?
options: The test checks only the first letter
feedback: Both strings match until their common end.
Comparison proceeds to a difference or end of string.

selfcheck.prompt: Why validate input before calling strcmp?
options: To establish a '\0' within the available array
To make strcmp always return exactly -1, 0 or 1
To substitute strlen for the buffer check
feedback: The function requires C strings. Establish their boundaries first.
The contract specifies the sign or zero.

selfcheck.prompt: Why does OK! pass a two-byte prefix test and fail an exact match against OK?
selfcheck.feedback: The opening bytes O and K match. The whole-string comparison finds a difference at position 2, where the bytes are ! and '\0'.

practice.title: Recognize the controller keys
practice.task: Read only the first record. If it has up to eight bytes and matches OK or ADJ exactly, print known, a space and the length. Other valid text, including an empty line, gives unknown. Print invalid for an empty stream, a record longer than eight bytes or a record containing NUL. LF and CRLF separators are excluded from the length. EOF can end the final record. Keep the supplied read_line validation and correct the key comparison.
practice.hint: The reader already checks the buffer boundary. Which comparison includes information about the byte after a matching prefix?
criteria: OK gives known 2, ADJ gives known 3, and OK! and ADJx give unknown.
A record of eight bytes is valid input. Nine bytes give invalid.
An embedded null or missing record gives invalid. Library functions receive only accepted text.
Cases marked “automatic WASI check” use exact bytes. Read their labels and expected output. You can enter the other cases in the lesson editor.

steps.why: An extra character distinguishes a key from its prefix.

steps.action: Correct the key test and rerun the same input.
steps.why: An exact key shares the position of the string end.

steps.action: Run separate tests for OK, ADJ, eight digits and nine digits.
steps.why: These inputs separate key recognition from the length limit.
steps.expected: The results are known 2, known 3, unknown and invalid.

exercises.title: Try it on your own
exercises.task: In the lesson editor, after saving a copy of main.c in a separate text file, change the dictionary to RUN and STOP and keep the limit. Check the labelled WASI cases against their expected output. Restore your saved main.c after the experiment.
criteria: RUN and STOP give known 3 and known 4.
RUN! gives unknown. Invalid length produces invalid before comparison.
